summary: This informational memo describes challenges of securing resource-constrained smart object devices. It describes a possible deployment model where such devices sign message objects, discusses the availability of cryptographic libraries for them, and presents some implementation experience.

eli5.summary: Tiny gadgets have little memory, but still need locks. This tells what was tried to give them signing powers and what was hard.

questions: how to secure constrained iot devices
what is ecc and why is it better
how do you provision keys on devices with no interface
subtitle: Resource-constrained IoT devices can implement cryptographic security despite memory and power limitations.

tldr.problem: Smart object networks face three challenges: implementing cryptographic security on devices with limited RAM, processor power and storage; provisioning keys and identities on devices with no user interface; and choosing the right security layer when the network has middleboxes that must cache or transform data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a deployment model using self-generated secure identities (like Cryptographically Generated Addresses), discusses available cryptographic libraries and implementation performance, presents a proof-of-concept using public-key cryptography on Arduino, and analyzes design trade-offs including freshness, layering, and symmetric versus asymmetric cryptography.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now understand that asymmetric cryptography is feasible on constrained devices with careful implementation; elliptic curve cryptography outperforms RSA; and data-object layer security can work alongside middleboxes for sleeping sensors.

facts.label: Test platforms used
facts.value: Arduino Uno (8-bit) and ARM Cortex-M boards (32-bit)

today: RFC 8387 is an Informational RFC documenting practical experiences in securing resource-constrained IoT devices. It remains highly relevant as the Internet of Things grows, providing evidence-based guidance that elliptic curve cryptography is practical on smart objects and proposing provisioning models that minimize configuration burden while maintaining security.

sections.title: The Three Challenges of Smart Object Security
sections.content: Smart objects (resource-constrained IoT devices) face three intersecting challenges. First, implementation difficulty: these devices have limited processor speed, RAM (often measured in kilobytes), and flash storage. Implementing full cryptographic stacks is hard. Second, provisioning: devices typically have no keyboard or display, making it nearly impossible to manually install security credentials. Manual configuration does not scale when there are dozens or hundreds of devices. Third, layering: sensor networks often use intermediaries (brokers, caches, aggregators) that must be awake when the sensor is asleep. End-to-end IP or transport-layer security does not fit this model; data-object layer security is needed instead.
sections.eli5: Imagine a tiny weather sensor with a coin battery and no buttons. How do you give it the ability to sign its measurements, get it to trust who it talks to, and let a caching server hold its data while it sleeps?

sections.title: A Self-Generated Identity Approach
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a practical deployment model centered on self-generated secure identities. Each device generates its own asymmetric key pair and derives an identity from it (similar to Cryptographically Generated Addresses in RFC 3972). These identities are self-authenticating: if you know the identity, a message signed with the corresponding private key proves it came from that device.

At installation time, personnel simply scan or record the identities of devices as they are physically placed (e.g., which sensor goes in which room). The installation process notes these short identity strings, not complex certificates or shared secrets. Once a server knows which identities are authorized, sensors can send signed messages and the server can verify them without prior secret exchange. New identities can be generated at factory reset or ownership transfer to limit tracking. For multi-device kits, group identities (hashes of all device public keys) allow registering entire sets at once.
sections.eli5: Instead of a complex setup, each device picks a number that proves who it is. At installation, you just write down the numbers. Later, messages with a proof matching the number are trusted.

sections.title: Performance and Cryptographic Libraries
sections.content:
The RFC surveys available asymmetric cryptographic libraries: AVRCryptoLib (3.6 kB, RSA and AES), TinyECC (sensor-optimized ECC), Relic-toolkit (flexible, supports RSA/ECC/pairing), Wiselib (C++ template library), and MatrixSSL (low-footprint TLS). Key finding: asymmetric cryptography code is surprisingly compact at 3.6 to 29 kB of flash.

Implementation experiences on Arduino (8-bit, 2 kB RAM, 32 kB flash) and ARM Cortex platforms show that RSA with 2048-bit keys is prohibitively slow (over 26 minutes on 8-bit). Elliptic Curve Cryptography vastly outperforms RSA: ECDSA with secp192r1 took ~3.6 ms on Arduino, versus 1.5+ million ms for RSA-2048. On 32-bit ARM Cortex-M, ECDSA times range from 200 to 1600 ms. Curves Curve25519 and edwards25519 are especially efficient: Ed25519 signatures take ~1.5 seconds on Arduino. The lesson: asymmetric cryptography is feasible with careful algorithm selection. 32-bit microcontrollers are recommended for real deployments; they are now cheaper and more power-efficient than 8-bit chips. Processing power and randomness sources are critical concerns.
sections.eli5: ECC is much faster than RSA on tiny devices. A modern chip can sign in a fraction of a second. The trick is picking the right curve and having a good random number generator.

sections.title: Working Example and Design Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The RFC describes a working prototype with an Arduino sensor running CoAP and Relic cryptography; a publish-subscribe broker caching readings; a resource directory; and an application retrieving data. At boot, the sensor generates keys and registers with its public key. When measuring data, it signs the measurement using JOSE or COSE before sending to the broker. Verification happens asynchronously, proving end-to-end security despite caching intermediaries.

Three critical design trade-offs emerge. Freshness and replay protection: sequence numbers in signed messages prevent replays but require broker state tracking. Timestamps add assurance of creation time, but constrained devices struggle to maintain accurate clocks without consuming energy on NTP. Security layering: link layer (Wi-Fi WPA) offers no end-to-end protection; network layer (IPsec) stops at middleboxes; data-object layer protects individual elements and works best with intermediaries like brokers. Symmetric versus asymmetric cryptography: symmetric keys are fast but require complex provisioning; public-key cryptography via self-generated identities eliminates provisioning burden. For sensors with sleeping intermediaries, data-object public-key signing is preferred. For session-based protocols like DTLS, key exchange followed by symmetric encryption is efficient.
sections.eli5: The sensor signs its temperature reading like signing a letter. Brokers cache it and others verify. Three trade-offs matter: How do you stop old messages being replayed? At which network layer should you lock things? When is speed (symmetric) worth setup burden (asymmetric)?

sections.title: Key Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes recommendations for developers and product designers:

Hardware selection should follow security requirements, not the reverse. Choose the processor first, then pick a platform with sufficient power to run the cryptography you need.

Favor ECC over RSA for constrained devices. The performance difference is dramatic.

Cryptographic randomness is non-negotiable. Use hardware random number generators; software pseudo-random on limited platforms is risky for key generation.

Use 32-bit microcontrollers. They are cheaper, more power-efficient, and more programmer-friendly than 8-bit chips.

Plan for firmware updates. Reserve at least double the code size in flash memory for firmware upgrades.

Enable identity rotation. Provide mechanisms for devices to generate new identities at factory reset or ownership change.
sections.eli5: Pick your chip based on security needs, not budget. Use modern ECC, not old RSA. Insist on a proper random number source. Use 32-bit chips. Plan room for updates. Let devices pick new identities if resold.
